Just had a chance to host a chat with @emollick about his upcoming book, Co-Existence. It is going to be a hit and is full of practical insights on AI. There will be many positive reviews of the ideas, but let me suggest three non-obvious meta-reasons to read it sooner rather than later:
1. How to work (co-exist?) with AI. Every so often, Ethan pulls back the curtain and describes how he uses AI in the book writing process. You get a peek into specific techniques and, more importantly, the mindset that will make someone successful.
2. The Mollick production function. The book is long enough to give Ethan breathing room to show why he's such a different thinker and fun to hang out with. He actually plays with the tools for long enough to get a finger-feel for what's possible (that's why he is texting at 2 am!); he constantly conceptualizes what he's encountering (jagged frontier, leadership-crowd-lab, the multi-player 2x2, etc.), pushing the ideas to their logical (and often uncomfortable) conclusion; and he ruthlessly throws away ideas when they no longer match the facts on the ground (especially important as everything changes so rapidly).
3. Common knowledge. In this time of hyper-personalized bubbles, we forget the value in having a shared set of stories, frameworks, and ideas. Ethan's book is going to be read by everyone from CEOs to ambitious high schoolers. The book is going to be referenced at many business meetings and holiday dinners so you might as well join in the fun early so you can give a knowing look when someone tells his escalator vs eschaton story, explains the best reasons not to use AI, or debates StrongDM-style software factories.

I spent a decent amount of time with Gemini 4 before launch. Overall, Gemini 4 is a big jump over previous Gemini models and it is the first non-OpenAI/Anthropic model to pass the Fable/Mythos/Astra bar. It is also much more pleasant and more agentic then previous Gemini models, without the weird personality issues that you often found in Gemini 3 series models. In fact, a big advantage is that has a very different personality and sense of taste than Claude or Astra, making it a good addition to the AI world. 

On the usefulness side, in some areas it is at least at par with OpenAI and Anthropic (it is quite creative and a good writer), but in others it lags, including at complex multi-agent work. It has a tendency to be too certain about its conclusions and a little lazy, issues not helped by the Antigravity harness not being quite as good as the competition. Still, I expect to see rapid improvements in model abilities using Gemini 4 as a base.

Here is a fun example:  "create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and inuitive to people who just want to play, but are sophisticated and deep for people who know something about architecture. you should be able to play a lot with design and approach. there should be simulation modes and different ways to view or experience the city. make it stunning. i want to host this on netlify in the end"

quoted_tweet.author: Robert Youssef
quoted_tweet.text:
People losing so much tokens and have no idea about this:

Subagent caches expire in five minutes.

In Claude Code, a subagent that sits idle longer than 5 minutes loses its prompt cache. The next call rewrites the whole context from scratch and burns several times more tokens than a cache hit would.

Anthropic's guide covers a single setting that stretches that window to an hour:

"subagentPromptCacheTtl": "1h"

The trade-off is in the write price. Each write to the 1-hour cache costs more than a write to the 5-minute one. You stop paying for a full rewrite every time a subagent pauses, though.

For workflows with long gaps between subagent calls, the savings reportedly reach up to 25% of total token spend.

Those savings depend heavily on how you work. If your subagents finish fast and rarely sit idle past five minutes, you pay the pricier write for nothing and your bill goes up.

Check your own usage before you switch. A comparison script exists that estimates whether the 1-hour TTL saves you money or costs you more on your actual sessions. If your pauses stay under five minutes, keep the default.

i love writing. i never let agents write for me. whether it's docs, or tweets, or shitposts, or even prompts (okay maybe that one's harder as agents manage other agents) 

there's a simple reason for that: i still strongly believe that writing is thinking. it's a skill i hope to never give up. it's also important to me that whatever i say is always authentic, mistakes and all. my favorite posts are the ones that i just full send without any editing

i suspect it also helps with prompting. being able to clearly express what i want, and knowing the vocabulary i need to be able to direct my agents does seem to make for more effective usage of agents. in the same way that engineers have an advantage when we prompt agents to write code, because we are intimately familiar with the words that make up the discipline

knowing the right word incantations to get an agent to produce a desired goal almost feels like spellcasting. as models get more capable, and that input box looks more and more like a magic box that can output anything, words become the interface between you and the genie

there may come a time when we give up the keyboard in exchange for brain-computer interfaces. but until then, i'm writing every word.

Had early access to Gemini 4 Argon - so I asked for slides on the AI power bottleneck.

It synthesized 8 years of 10-K filings, FERC queue data across all 6 US grid operators, 17 gigawatt cluster buildouts, and a decade of GPU thermal specs.

And I got this interactive deck 🤯

Asked Gemini 4 Argon for an interactive museum of Apple computers.

...and didn't provide any images or data.

It scraped archival Mac photos, wrote a tool to clean the images, pulled 50 years of specs, and built a 3D Cover Flow with UI that morphs to match the decade you’re in.

quoted_tweet.author: Logan Kilpatrick
quoted_tweet.text:
Today we are rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally in the Gemini API, to Pro + Ultra in Gemini App, and Ultra subs in Antigravity!

Argon is a huge step forward for Gemini, and a labor of love. This model has been battle tested by over 100,000 people at Google over the last month, with so much new innovation, ambition, and hard work baked into this release. The team has been heads down over the last 6 months working to make this possible across the stack (research, infra, safety, eng, etc).

We rolled the model out to cyber defenders as part of our fairwind program and early access customers over the last 2 weeks, it has been amazing to see and talk to folks who are now using this model daily. Seeing the models writing capability, raw knowledge and persistence for coding, paired with new features like 1M token output when the model needs to work more has gotten me even more excited about our path ahead.

This is just the start of the Gemini 4 era. As you saw with 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash, our iteration speed with Gemini is fast : ) Now with Gemini 4 Argon to work from, I am cannot wait to see the progress continue, and most importantly see what this new model enables for the world. 

This is such a special moment in the arc of technology, as millions of people everyday tackle problems they could never have thought possible before. Gemini 4 Argon was built to help you tackle the hardest problems. I have personally felt this spark with Argon and hope you do too. Onwards!!
